questions.question: Prying forces are:
options: shearing forces on the bolts because of the joints
tensile forces due to the flexibility of connected parts
bending forces on the bolts because of the joints
forces due the friction between connected parts

structuredOptions.label: A
structuredOptions.text: shearing forces on the bolts because of the joints
structuredOptions.html: shearing forces on the bolts because of the joints

structuredOptions.label: B
structuredOptions.text: tensile forces due to the flexibility of connected parts
structuredOptions.html: tensile forces due to the flexibility of connected parts

structuredOptions.label: C
structuredOptions.text: bending forces on the bolts because of the joints
structuredOptions.html: bending forces on the bolts because of the joints

structuredOptions.label: D
structuredOptions.text: forces due the friction between connected parts
structuredOptions.html: forces due the friction between connected parts

questions.explanation:
Steel Structures | Bolted Connections

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Recall
  • Given Data: The term "Prying forces" in structural joints.
  • Aim: Identify the mechanical cause and nature of prying forces from the given options.

3. Core Concepts:

Prying Action: In bolted connections subjected to direct tension (like a T-stub or an angle bracket), the connected flexible parts deform/bend under the tensile load. Because of this bending, the edges/tips of the connected parts pivot and press hard against each other (or against the supporting member). This leverage creates an additional reaction force, which in turn significantly increases the tensile force applied to the bolts beyond the primary externally applied tension.

Hence, prying forces are additional tensile forces induced directly due to the flexibility (bending/deformation) of the connected parts.

4. Solution Method:

Reviewing the options against the definition:

  • (A) Shearing forces: Incorrect — prying acts in tension.
  • (B) Tensile forces due to flexibility of connected parts: ✓ Correct definition.
  • (C) Bending forces on the bolts: Incorrect — though the plate bends, the resultant prying force on the bolt is pure tension.
  • (D) Friction forces: Incorrect — friction relates to slip-critical shear joints.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Conceptual verification strictly aligns with Option (B).

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: Tensile forces due to the flexibility of connected parts  |  Correct option: (B)

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q44
questions.subject: Concrete & Steel Structures
questions.topic: Steel Tension, Compression Members & Plastic Analysis
questions.question: According to the concept of Limit State Design as per IS 456: 2000, the probability of failure of a structure is _____________.
questions.explanation:
Structural Engineering | Limit State Design

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Comprehension
  • Given Data: Limit State Design concept as per IS 456:2000.
  • Aim: Determine the theoretical probability of failure of a structure.

3. Core Concepts:

In Limit State Design (probabilistic approach), both the material strength and the loads are assumed to follow a normal distribution curve.

  • Characteristic Strength (\(f_{ck}\)): The strength below which not more than 5% of the test results are expected to fall. Thus, the probability of actual strength being less than characteristic strength is \(P_S = 0.05\).
  • Characteristic Load (\(L_c\)): The load which has a 95% probability of not being exceeded during the life of the structure. Thus, the probability of the actual load exceeding the characteristic load is \(P_L = 0.05\).

For a structure to be definitively safe, two independent events must happen simultaneously: (1) the load must be less than the characteristic load, and (2) the material strength must be greater than the characteristic strength.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Probability of safety concerning load \(= 1 - P_L = 1 - 0.05 = 0.95\)
  2. Probability of safety concerning strength \(= 1 - P_S = 1 - 0.05 = 0.95\)
  3. Overall probability of safety \(= 0.95 \times 0.95 = 0.9025\)
  4. Theoretical probability of failure:\[P_f = 1 - 0.9025 = 0.0975 \]

6. Final Answer:

Final Answer: 0.0975  |  Accepted key range: 0.09 to 0.10

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q45
questions.subject: Concrete & Steel Structures
questions.topic: Limit State Design of Beams & Slabs
questions.question: In a pre-stressed concrete beam section shown in the figure, the net loss is 10% and the final pre-stressing force applied at \(X\) is 750 kN. The initial fiber stresses (in N/mm²) at the top and bottom of the beam were:
questions.explanation:
Structural Engineering | Prestressed Concrete

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Application
  • Given Data:
    • Cross-section: \(b = 250\) mm, Total depth \(D = 200 + 200 = 400\) mm.
    • Final prestressing force applied at X: \(P_f = 750\) kN.
    • Distance of X from bottom fiber: \(d_2 = 100\) mm.
    • Net loss of prestress \(= 10\%\).
  • Aim: Initial fiber stresses at the top and bottom of the beam.

3. Core Concepts:

  • Centroid and Eccentricity: The centroidal axis passes through the mid-depth (\(y = D/2 = 200\) mm from top/bottom). The force is applied at 100 mm from the bottom, so its eccentricity \(e = 200 - 100 = 100\) mm below the neutral axis.
  • Initial Force: Since losses are 10%, the final force is 90% of the initial force: \(P_f = 0.9\, P_i\).
  • Combined Stresses: Stresses at any fiber are the sum of direct axial stress (\(P/A\)) and bending stress (\(M/Z\)). Compressive stresses are taken as positive.

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

  1. Initial Prestressing Force (\(P_i\)):\[P_i = \frac{P_f}{0.9} = \frac{750}{0.9} = 833.333 \text{ kN} = 833.333 \times 10^3 \text{ N} \]
  2. Section Properties:\[A = 250 \times 400 = 100{,}000 \text{ mm}^2 \]\[Z = \frac{bD^2}{6} = \frac{250 \times 400^2}{6} = 6.667 \times 10^6 \text{ mm}^3 \]
  3. Stresses due to Initial Prestress:\[\sigma_d = \frac{P_i}{A} = \frac{833.333 \times 10^3}{100{,}000} = 8.333 \text{ MPa} \]\[M = P_i \times e = 833.333 \times 10^3 \times 100 = 83.333 \times 10^6 \text{ N·mm} \]\[\sigma_b = \frac{M}{Z} = \frac{83.333 \times 10^6}{6.667 \times 10^6} = 12.50 \text{ MPa} \]
  4. Resultant Initial Fiber Stresses:
    Top fiber (force acts below centroid → tension at top):\[\sigma_{top} = \sigma_d - \sigma_b = 8.333 - 12.50 = -4.167 \text{ MPa (Tension)} \]Bottom fiber (force causes compression at bottom):\[\sigma_{bot} = \sigma_d + \sigma_b = 8.333 + 12.50 = 20.833 \text{ MPa (Compression)} \]

6. Final Answer:

Correct option: (D)

questions.title: GATE CE 2015 Set 2 | CE Q46
questions.subject: Concrete & Steel Structures
questions.topic: Bond, Shear & Torsion in RCC
questions.question: A fixed end beam is subjected to a load, W at 1/3rd span from the left support as shown in the figure. The collapse load of the beam is:
questions.explanation:
Structural Engineering | Structural Analysis (Plastic Analysis)

2. Problem Analysis:

  • Taxonomy: Analysis
  • Given Data:
    • Fixed beam of span \(L\) with point load \(W\) at \(L/3\) from left support \(X\).
    • Left half capacity (\(0\) to \(L/2\)): \(2M_P\)
    • Right half capacity (\(L/2\) to \(L\)): \(M_P\)
  • Aim: Determine the collapse load \(W_c\).

3. Core Concepts:

We must check the Kinematic method for the most critical collapse mechanism. Potential plastic hinge locations are at the supports (\(X, Z\)), under the load (\(C\)), and at the change of cross-section (\(Y\)).

5. Step-by-Step Execution:

Mechanism 1 (Hinges at X, C, Z):
Let displacement at \(C\) be \(\delta\).\[\theta_X = \frac{\delta}{L/3} = \frac{3\delta}{L}, \quad \theta_Z = \frac{\delta}{2L/3} = \frac{1.5\delta}{L} \]Hinge rotation at \(C = \theta_X + \theta_Z = \dfrac{4.5\delta}{L}\)
Internal Work (capacities \(2M_P\) at \(X\), \(2M_P\) at \(C\), \(M_P\) at \(Z\)):\[W_I = (2M_P)\frac{3\delta}{L} + (2M_P)\frac{4.5\delta}{L} + (M_P)\frac{1.5\delta}{L} = 16.5\frac{M_P\delta}{L} \]External Work: \(W_E = W\delta \implies W_c = 16.5\dfrac{M_P}{L}\)

Mechanism 2 (Hinges at X, Y, Z):
Due to the abrupt reduction in capacity at \(Y\) (midspan), a hinge forms at \(Y\) instead of under the load. Let displacement at \(Y\) be \(\Delta\).\[\theta_X = \frac{\Delta}{L/2} = \frac{2\Delta}{L}, \quad \theta_Z = \frac{2\Delta}{L}, \quad \text{Hinge rotation at } Y = \frac{4\Delta}{L} \]Internal Work (capacities \(2M_P\) at \(X\), \(M_P\) at \(Y\), \(M_P\) at \(Z\)):\[W_I = (2M_P)\frac{2\Delta}{L} + (M_P)\frac{4\Delta}{L} + (M_P)\frac{2\Delta}{L} = 10\frac{M_P\Delta}{L} \]Displacement at \(C\) (by similar triangles) \(= \dfrac{L/3}{L/2}\Delta = \dfrac{2\Delta}{3}\)\[W_E = W\left(\frac{2\Delta}{3}\right) \]Equating:\[W\left(\frac{2\Delta}{3}\right) = 10\frac{M_P\Delta}{L} \implies W_c = 15.0\frac{M_P}{L} \]Validation: The bending moment at \(C\) for Mechanism 2 is \(1.667M_P\), well below its local capacity of \(2M_P\). Yield conditions are satisfied. Mechanism 2 gives the lower (critical) collapse load.

6. Final Answer:

Correct option: (C)  \(W_c = 15.0\,M_P/L\)
